blocks.content:
Explore is Grafana's ad-hoc query and investigation workspace — no dashboard required. This guide walks through:

- Installing a shared set of demo data sources, so every step below works identically for everyone
- The shared interface: toolbar, query row, and results controls that work the same everywhere
- Querying **metrics** with PromQL
- Querying **logs** with LogQL
- Querying **traces** with TraceQL

Each section ends with links to go deeper.

Install a small set of free, Grafana-hosted demo data sources first — real metrics, logs, and traces from the same sample app, so this guide behaves identically no matter what you've already connected.

blocks.title: Install the shared demo data sources

blocks.content: Click **Demo Data Dashboards** in the main menu.

blocks.tooltip: QuickPizza is a small, fully-instrumented demo app hosted by Grafana — querying it never counts toward your usage.
blocks.content: Click **Install the Quick Pizza SRE demo**. This adds matching Prometheus, Loki, and Tempo data sources and refreshes the page.
You now have **grafanacloud-play-prom**, **grafanacloud-play-logs**, and **grafanacloud-play-traces** — the same real demo data used in every section below.
Start by touring the controls that stay the same no matter which data source you query.
Click **Explore** in the main menu.

blocks.reftarget: div[data-testid='data-testid Data source picker select container']
blocks.tooltip: Every query starts here — Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, or anything else you've connected.
blocks.content: Find the data source picker at the top left of the toolbar.

blocks.hint: This shortcut only appears for data sources with a matching drilldown app installed.
blocks.tooltip: It opens a purpose-built drilldown view for the same data source without writing a query.
blocks.content: Notice the **Go queryless** shortcut next to the data source picker.
Click **Split** to open a second, independent query pane.
Split view is ideal for comparing two queries, two data sources, or two time ranges side by side.
Click the close icon on the new pane to return to a single pane.

blocks.tooltip: Use it to open another data source in a new tab without losing your current query.
blocks.content: Notice **Add**, for opening additional Explore tabs.

blocks.tooltip: The arrows on either side step that same range backward or forward, and the magnifying glass zooms out.
blocks.content: The time range picker controls the window every query runs against.
Click **Run query** to execute whatever is in the query editor.

blocks.tooltip: Handy for watching something unfold in near-real time without clicking Run query yourself.
blocks.content: Next to it, the refresh-interval control turns on auto-refresh.

blocks.tooltip: Anyone who opens it lands on the same data source, query, and time range you're looking at.
blocks.content: **Share** copies a link that reproduces this exact query and time range.
Click **Outline** to toggle the section-jump sidebar.

blocks.tooltip: Later queries can reference an earlier one's results by that letter — useful for math across queries.
blocks.content: Each query lives in its own row, labeled **A**, **B**, and so on.

blocks.tooltip: Its neighbors let you view data source help, save the query, hide its results, remove it, or drag it to reorder.
blocks.content: Icons on the query row include a duplicate-query shortcut, shown here.
Click **Query history** to see every query you've run recently.
Browse history by day, star favorites, or filter by data source.
Click **Query history** again to close the panel.
Click **Query inspector** to inspect the raw request and response.
Its Stats, Query, JSON, and Data tabs show timing, the exact request sent, and the payload returned — invaluable when a query doesn't behave as expected.
Click **Query inspector** again to close it.
You now know every shared control in Explore — from picking a data source to comparing two queries side by side.
Prometheus and other metrics data sources speak PromQL. Select one to build your first metrics query.
Open the data source picker and select **grafanacloud-play-prom**.

blocks.tooltip: A quick way to insert a common query shape — rate, histogram, or similar — instead of starting from a blank editor.
blocks.content: **Kick start your query** offers ready-made PromQL patterns.

blocks.tooltip: Type a few letters and it fuzzy-searches every metric name your Prometheus data source knows about.
blocks.content: In **Builder** mode, the Metric field searches available metric names as you type.

blocks.tooltip: Browse by name or type, and read each metric's description before you commit to it.
blocks.content: The book icon opens a full, searchable catalog of every available metric.

blocks.tooltip: Label filters narrow a metric down to a specific service, instance, or any other dimension it's tagged with.
blocks.content: **Label filters** let you scope a metric to exactly the series you care about.

blocks.tooltip: This is the same function library PromQL uses — rate, sum, histogram_quantile, and dozens more — applied visually.
blocks.content: **Operations** adds functions to your query without typing PromQL by hand.

blocks.reftarget: div[data-testid='data-testid prometheus explain switch wrapper'] div[data-testid='data-testid Switch container']
blocks.content: Turn on **Explain** to see your query broken down in plain English.

blocks.reftarget: div[data-testid='data-testid Query editor row prometheus A']
blocks.tooltip: Each clause gets its own numbered, plain-language explanation — useful while you're still learning PromQL.
blocks.content: Explain mode annotates every part of the query above the editor.

blocks.reftarget: div[data-testid='data-testid prometheus explain switch wrapper'] div[data-testid='data-testid Switch container']
blocks.content: Turn **Explain** back off.
Switch to **Code** mode to write raw PromQL directly.

blocks.tooltip: It walks you through picking a metric, then narrowing it down by label, without memorizing PromQL syntax.
blocks.content: **Metrics browser** builds a query for you from labels, step by step.

blocks.tooltip: It's a counter from the shared demo app — one of the same metrics every Grafana Cloud user just installed.
blocks.content: Type `quickpizza_server_http_request_duration_seconds_count`.
Click **Run query**.
A counter like this only ever goes up, so it's more useful as a rate. Wrap it in `rate(...)` to see requests per second instead.
Replace the query with `rate(quickpizza_server_http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])`.
Click **Run query** again.

blocks.tooltip: Lines suit trends over time; bars and points can make sparse or discrete values easier to read.
blocks.content: Results render as a **Graph**, with Lines, Bars, Points, and stacked variants in the top-right corner.

blocks.tooltip: Click one to isolate it, or shift-click to build up a custom comparison of just the series you want.
blocks.content: The legend below the graph lists every series, with its full label set.

blocks.tooltip: Toggle to Table for a spreadsheet-style view of the exact same data.
blocks.content: **Raw** shows the underlying data frame — every returned series and its labels.
Expand **Options** to see legend, format, and query-type settings.

blocks.tooltip: Instant returns one value per series for the end of the time range — useful for current-state checks like this one.
blocks.content: **Type** switches between a full time series (**Range**), a single point (**Instant**), or **Both**.
You wrote, explained, and visualized a PromQL query, and know where its display and query-type options live.
Loki and other log data sources speak LogQL. Select one to search and filter real log lines.
Open the data source picker and select **grafanacloud-play-logs**.

blocks.tooltip: It inserts a ready-made LogQL pattern instead of starting from a blank query.
blocks.content: **Kick start your query** offers common LogQL patterns here too.

blocks.tooltip: It lists every label Loki knows about, with autocomplete for values, so you can build a selector without memorizing names.
blocks.content: **Label browser** is Loki's dedicated tool for discovering labels and values.
Click **Select label** to see the labels available on your logs.
Choose **service_name**, then set its value to **quickpizza-catalog** — a real service in the shared demo dataset. Every Loki query starts with a label selector like this in curly braces.

blocks.tooltip: It's the LogQL equivalent of grep — keep only lines that contain (or don't contain) a given string.
blocks.content: Every new query starts with a **Line contains** filter, ready to narrow results further.
Type `doughs` into the line filter — one of QuickPizza's real API paths — to match only lines containing it.
Click **Run query**.

Above the results, Loki shows how much data it scanned and often suggests hints like **add json parser** — one click adds a parser for structured log lines. QuickPizza's logs are JSON and include a `traceID` field — the same trace you'll open in the next section.

blocks.hint: Some Loki versions label this panel slightly differently — continue if it isn't found.
blocks.tooltip: Spikes and quiet periods here often point straight at when an incident started.
blocks.content: **Logs volume** charts how many lines matched per time bucket, broken down by level.

blocks.tooltip: Checking one adds it as its own column, and the percentage shows how many of the returned lines actually have it.
blocks.content: The left-hand fields panel lists every field detected in your log lines.
Click the menu icon on a log line to see what you can do with it.
From here you can show full log details, view surrounding context lines, pin the line, copy it as text or JSON, or ask Grafana Assistant to explain it.
Click **Live** to start tailing new log lines as they arrive.
Click it again to stop and return to a normal query.

blocks.hint: If this isn't found, look for a similar collapsed **Options** row above the results.
blocks.content: Expand **Options** to see the line limit and read direction.
You built a label selector, filtered lines by content, inspected fields, and tailed logs live.
Tempo and other tracing data sources speak TraceQL. Select one to search traces and drill into individual spans.
Open the data source picker and select **grafanacloud-play-traces**.

blocks.tooltip: Search is form-based, TraceQL is a query language for precise filters, and Service Graph shows dependencies between services.
blocks.content: Tempo offers three query types: **Search**, **TraceQL**, and **Service Graph**.

blocks.reftarget: div[data-testid='data-testid Query editor row tempo A'] div[data-testid='data-testid RadioGroup container'] div[data-testid='data-testid radio-button']:contains('Search')
blocks.content: Select **Search** for a form-based way to find traces.
Set **Service Name** to `quickpizza-public-api` — a real, traced service in the shared demo dataset. **Span Name**, **Status**, **Duration**, and **Tags** filter further the same way.

blocks.tooltip: Every filter you set in the form above is expressed as a single TraceQL expression here.
blocks.content: **Edit in TraceQL** drops you into the raw query behind your form selections.
Click **Run query** to search for matching traces.

blocks.tooltip: Each row is one trace: a single end-to-end request across every service it touched.
blocks.content: Matching traces list as a table, with trace ID, start time, service, name, and duration.

blocks.hint: No traces matched — widen the time range or clear the Service Name filter, then try again.
blocks.content: Click the first **Trace ID** to open its full waterfall view.

blocks.tooltip: The route is the entry span's name — usually the endpoint or operation the request started at.
blocks.content: The trace header shows total duration, how many services were involved, and the route.
Just below the header, **Overview** shows a mini waterfall of the whole trace for quick orientation — collapse it once you've found the section you want to zoom into.

blocks.tooltip: Critical path highlights the spans that actually determined total trace duration; the others surface likely problem spots.
blocks.content: Filter spans by attribute or text, or use the **Critical path**, **Errors**, and **High latency** shortcuts.
Click the first span to expand its details.
A span's details include its own attributes, resource attributes (service, cluster, region, and more), and a **Related logs** button that jumps straight to log lines from the same request.

blocks.reftarget: div[data-testid='data-testid Query editor row tempo A'] div[data-testid='data-testid RadioGroup container'] div[data-testid='data-testid radio-button']:contains('Service Graph')
blocks.content: Switch to **Service Graph** to see how services depend on each other.
Click **Run query** to build the graph.
Each node shows request rate and error rate for that service, and each edge is a dependency between two services — a fast way to spot where errors or latency are concentrated across a whole system.
You searched for traces, opened a trace's waterfall, inspected a span's attributes, and viewed the service dependency graph.
